And frankly, instead of just sending a representative, people sent their CEOs or general councils. And I mean, we had, you know, really the biggest names, not just in crypto, but in, you know, venture capital, you know, Nasdaq, State Street, Fidelity, big companies trying to deal with custody issues and how to introduce this to retail investors in a way. So it was incredibly well received. And so we came out of that. That was the piece that got us a lot of momentum. So following that roundtable, we started working together, Darren Soto and I in particular, on how to craft a bill that was the consensus afterwards. And really at the last meeting, Darren asked a good question. He said, why would this become a partisan issue? It's really from the participants in attendance and the members on the panel and staff that were there, it was clear that it really had nothing to do with partisanship. It was really whether you actually understood the issue or not. So we left pretty optimistic that we would be able to spread this out and get some momentum with the legislation. And it took longer than we thought to kind of get the consensus together. And so we said, well, by the end of the year, we'll do it. Then at the start of the next Congress, we'll introduce it as a new piece of legislation. And so we did that and we got a feedback period and we thought, well, we'll get a little bit of feedback and we'll probably introduce it in February. They have innovative ideas here. A lot of their talent is here. We have the right infrastructure here, but we don't have the framework to do the investment. And they really want what a lot of people feared with Facebook is that they would filter their financial transactions the same way they've started filtering speech or content.
